title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Saturday morning, Nov 21
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:20 AM ET Saturday, Nov 21, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to close Rikers Island is still the Right's biggest story: the Rikers query matched 51,234 posts in 24 hours, 14,039 of them overnight, and both 'Rikers' and 'Mamdani' were trending in the U.S. The top overnight post quoted Rep. Brandon Gill: Democrats ran on affordability and are 'closing the prisons.' The plan actually keeps Rikers open until 2032, five years past the current legal deadline. New on the Right: Friday's AI-stock rout (Nasdaq −5.3%) is being blamed on Democrats. That query matched 9,842 posts (7.94× its prior average), led by a 119,550-view post saying 'Wall Street is getting absolutely DESTROYED by the Democrats.' Reporting ties the drop mainly to Nvidia and the Anthropic IPO, and the new Congress isn't sworn in until January. 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' doubled its prior average (3,247 posts). On the Far Left, 'Jeffries won't defund the war' held at 1,417 posts, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin's vote for Van Hollen kept the Schumer fight going (3,899 posts, cooling). The 'nullify the midterms' push faded overnight. Four faded cards were dropped. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 7:05 AM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Gaming dominated ('GTA 6,' 1,128,064 posts; 'Lucia,' 363,483; 'Rockstar,' 203,817), along with Putin (294,500), Russia (208,021), Amazon (273,073), Black Friday (148,461) and Thanksgiving (78,362). 'Rikers' (62,598 posts) and 'Mamdani' (156,080) match the Rikers closure plan, so the Rikers card received the trend bonus; it is the only scored card that did. 'Mamdani' also covers his Achilles injury, Movember mustache memes and the DSA donation video, so we did not credit it to any other card. 'Anthropic' (112,981) relates to Friday's market sell-off but is about the company's IPO, not the claim that Democrats caused the drop, so the market card did not get the trend bonus. 'Putin,' 'Russia,' 'Greenland' (16,889), 'Sinaloa' (39,682) and 'Leo Frank' (3,693) were not reviewed as opposition narratives this morning. Where a trend object had no tweet_count ('Servicio Meteorológico,' 'Gallos Blancos'), its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from the Right, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The Iran-funding and Van Hollen cards are tagged Far Left because the pressure on Jeffries and Schumer comes from the party's left, even though Slotkin is not on the left and some posts come from 'America First' accounts. The Social Security card stays tagged Right because the 'Ponzi scheme' frame is a Right talking point. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Saturday, Nov 21, 2026, 7:20 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:05 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 20, 5:20 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eleven of its fifteen narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM Friday ET), so we also report each query's 5 PM–7 AM ET overnight count against the same hours a night earlier. Four narratives were dropped because they faded: the resurfaced 2023 'We stand with Israel' clip (630 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.47× its prior daily average; 115 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 1,373 the same hours a night earlier); DSA and AOC 2028 (400 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.43× its prior daily average; 97 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 287 the same hours a night earlier); the 'third shutdown' threat (230 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.91× its prior daily average; 118 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 261 the same hours a night earlier); the reparations card (974 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.40× its prior daily average; 261 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 614 the same hours a night earlier). One was added with a new query: blaming Democrats for Friday's market drop. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: the filibuster and '60 votes' frustration on the left (564 posts, 0.49×); resurfaced claims that Mamdani's 2025 election was fraudulent, which Reuters and Lead Stories have called unverified per an X News summary (167 posts, 1.36×); and Mamdani's DSA donation video (50 posts on a donation-specific query).

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent twice: at daily granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 14, through 7:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 21 (the 'seven-day' total), and at hourly granularity over the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Friday, Nov 20, through 7:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 21). We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, advocacy groups, research groups, budget watchdogs, congressional committees, blogs, X News summaries, and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets. We re-researched the Rikers and Van Hollen cards this morning and added the outlets we retrieved to those cited last evening, which is why their outlet counts rose. The new market card counts the five outlets that covered Friday's sell-off (AP, Reuters, CNBC, NBC News, Axios); NPR and The Crosscheck are cited for Nov. 5 background but not counted. For the other cards the outlet count is carried over from last evening, and each says so. We noted whether each topic appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 7:05 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this morning. Only the Rikers card got the trend bonus. The Rikers and market queries had low baselines earlier in the week, so their acceleration indices are maxed out. The Van Hollen, popular-vote compact and rigged-midterms queries carry last week's spikes in their seven-day totals, which keeps their acceleration low. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Evening-to-morning score changes also reflect the higher volume ceiling (51,234 this morning versus 37,350 last evening) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The 'nullify' query overlaps the rigged-midterms query. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts that mention Democrats. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Social Security query also catches posts attacking Johnson. The immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A,' so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts. The Erie query includes the bare word 'Erie,' and this morning's sample showed unrelated Lake Erie and Erie County posts. The impeachment query also catches Democrats discussing impeachment. The rigged-midterms query also catches posts mocking fraud claims. The tax query catches generic complaints about state taxes. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the Rikers, market, Social Security, immigration and Erie queries. Other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Democrats crashed the stock market' is misleading. Friday's drop (Nasdaq −5.3%, S&P 500 −3.7%) was led by AI stocks after a reported SEC probe of Nvidia's accounting and a sell-off in Anthropic a day after its IPO (Reuters; CNBC; AP). Fear of Democratic limits on AI data centers is one factor analysts cite, but the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027, and The Crosscheck rated the same claim about the Nov. 5 drop Mixed. 'Mamdani's plan closes Rikers now' gets the timeline backward: the plan asks the City Council to move the legal deadline from August 2027 to the end of 2032, with benchmarks (City & State). Carried over from last evening: 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' (posts cite 2,100, 2,500 or 7,000) is misleading: the plan sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion, supervised release and shorter case delays, and Rikers stays open until borough jails are built (City of New York; Gothamist). Closing Rikers is not Mamdani's invention; a 2019 City Council law required it, and his plan moves the deadline later and still needs Council approval (AP). Whether the target can be met safely is a fair debate, which New York Post opinion writers dispute. 'Democrats' agenda is a $4.1 trillion tax hike' mixes up costs and taxes: CRFB's $4.1 trillion is a ten-year cost estimate, and its largest piece is repealing tariffs, which lowers taxes. The 'nullify the midterms' demand is still circulating; the president has no authority to cancel state results or declare martial law (Brennan Center; Protect Democracy), and fact-checkers found no evidence that machines switched votes. Posts using the Ian Murray case as proof that noncitizens are voting have no evidence behind them; 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading; 'Democrats are already preparing a third impeachment' is a prediction by Jim Jordan, not a report; CNBC's experts say the 'Ponzi scheme' label misses how Social Security is funded, and PolitiFact has rated the comparison False when others made it; 'Democrats are importing voters' runs into the law, since noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections; 'Jeffries backs the Iran war' is false as stated; and Lead Stories found no '30,000-case' Texas voter fraud probe.

The largest single item, $1.8 trillion, is repealing tariffs, which CRFB scores as lost revenue, and CRFB notes that repealing the 2025 tax cuts for high earners would raise about $2 trillion. talkingPoints: Democrats' 100-day agenda costs $4.1 trillion — guess who pays.
They ran on affordability and their first plan adds trillions to the debt.
Democrats always raise taxes; look at Minnesota, Colorado and Maryland.
Get ready for 'affordable' tax hikes.
Democrats won on affordability, and their first idea is raising your taxes.
39.6% is back on the table before they're even sworn in.
narratives.amplifiers: Named accounts in posts we opened: @GuntherEagleman (279 likes, 111 reposts, 14,435 views) and copy-paste versions from @real_jfkjr01 and @theletter17_; @Cmfover84 ('39.6% is back on the table,' 14 likes, 635 views); @Momo_Douk45 (423 views); and @PatriotAndPoise. X News kept its cluster updated overnight.
narratives.whyItWorks: Affordability won Democrats the midterms, so 'they'll raise your taxes' attacks the brand at its strongest point. It's also partly true — Democrats are debating tax increases — which makes the exaggeration ('on Americans') harder to rebut in one line.
narratives.audience: Conservative and libertarian voters, small-business owners, and swing voters who backed Democrats on costs. Also likely to resonate with moderate Democrats wary of the party's left.
narratives.counter: Say what the $4.1 trillion is: CRFB's ten-year estimate, and its biggest piece ($1.8 trillion) is ending Trump's tariffs, a tax cut for the people and businesses paying them. Then say who pays for the rest: CRFB itself notes that repealing the 2025 tax cuts for high earners would raise about $2 trillion. Say who pays. The proposals on the table target incomes over roughly $1 million and corporations, and Trump can veto all of it until 2029. Put the trade on the table plainly: restoring Medicaid, SNAP, and ACA subsidies for working families, paid for by the top bracket. Don't deny that a debate over tax increases is happening — it is.

factChecks.claim: Democrats are planning 'major tax hikes on Americans' for 2027.
factChecks.detail: The Wall Street Journal report, as quoted by Political Wire, says Democrats are 'weighing when to attach tax increases' to bills reversing Medicaid, SNAP, and health-subsidy cuts — a debate, not a passed plan. The Tax Foundation says the proposals on the table target high-income individuals and corporations and that any tax increase is 'limited by President Trump’s veto.' Viral posts dropped both caveats. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

talkingPoints: The 2026 election was run by an algorithm — the TV showed the algorithm's results, not real votes.
There was no blue wave. Texas did not turn blue.
20 million ghost voters with no proof of citizenship.
Machines, mail-in ballots, and non-citizens: the White House just admitted it.
Alaska's Senate seat was stolen with a decoy candidate.
narratives.amplifiers: Jerome Corsi's 'Voter Fraud Blue Wave' video, shared by many low-follower accounts; replies to @lancewallnau and @TrumpDailyPosts; X News summaries on Iowa and Texas. Counter-voice on the Right: @mitchellvii. No single fraud post in our sample passed a few hundred views.
narratives.whyItWorks: It protects identity after a defeat: if the loss was stolen, nothing has to change. Every glitch, late count, or unusual result becomes 'proof,' and Alaska's real dispute over a namesake candidate lends the broader claim borrowed credibility.
narratives.audience: Hard-core MAGA voters, election-denial communities that formed after 2020, and conservatives in states that flipped, such as Texas and Alaska.
narratives.counter: Lead with the scale: the swing was broad, it showed up in thousands of counties, and Republican candidates conceded. Then go claim by claim, using the fact-checks. Keep Alaska separate: a disputed ballot tactic is a real story, and treating it as proof of national fraud is the disinformation.

factChecks.claim: Iowa and Texas results prove the 2026 midterms were rigged.
factChecks.detail: Texas is running its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the Senate race, which compares a random sample of paper ballots with machine totals; it is a routine check required by 2021 state law, not a fraud investigation (Houston Public Media, KXAN). In Iowa, a candidate winning more votes than her party's registered voters is ordinary when independents and crossover voters back her. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Texas just opened a major investigation into 30,000 cases of voter fraud after the midterms.
factChecks.detail: Lead Stories found no announcement from the Texas Secretary of State and no news reports of such an investigation. The only post-midterm press release (Nov. 5) was about election-administration working groups. The '30,000' figure appears to echo a September Reuters story about non-citizens mistakenly added to voter rolls nationwide since 2000.

factChecks.claim: Texas Democrats 'found' 20 million new votes to flip the state blue.
factChecks.detail: Snopes found no proof for the claim and said it appeared to conflate an unproven claim about new voters nationwide with Texas alone. Based on Texas secretary of state figures, it said Democrats could not have 'found' 20 million people to tip the state's elections.

factChecks.claim: Inflated vote totals in Wyandot County, Ohio, prove election fraud.
factChecks.detail: AFP reports the county said vote totals from an Oct. 28 mock election were 'inadvertently left in the reporting system for one precinct,' which overreported unofficial totals for several races.
